Thus, if a single-syllable suffix is added to the root of such a word, stress would be on the ante-penultimate syllable.' with ['rana] / [ka-'rana-te], ['raka] / ['raka-ne], ['nio] / ['nio-ne], ['sani-m] / ['sani-ku]; then 'Words with a root of four or more syllables have secondary stress (") on the first syllable in addition to primary stress (') on the penu…
new_statements.relation_note: This is the very passage the catalog's full record for sout2895 ( : classification set by morphology, root-penult stress invariant under affixation, secondary stress on the first syllable of 4+-syllable roots, listed-set exceptions) is built from; the summary row in the target ('rule': '') is just the empty the rule as stated of that record. The quote was re-verified against the page image p. It refines the WALS coding (14A Penultimate, 15A Fixed), which is correct for bare roots but drops the root-domain (affix-invariant) condition.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root and stays there when prefixes or suffixes are added or removed (e.g. ['rana] 'grate' > [ka-'rana-te] 'grater'; ['raka] 'ocean' > ['raka-ne] 'outsider'; ['sani-ku] 'my shoulder'), so a root plus one suffix syllable carries word-antepenultimate stress and a prefixed monosyllabic root carries final stress. Stress is called phonemic but with a light functional load; syllable weight plays no role in the statement. For bare disyllabic roots the rule reduces to plain penultimate stress (the WALS coding).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Roots of four or more syllables take secondary stress on the first syllable of the root, with primary stress on the root penult: ["saka'hatɛ-nɛ] 'ghost', ["kupa'naha-ne] 'clove', ["kara'tupa] 'chili'. Nothing is said about secondary stress in shorter roots or on affix strings.
new_statements.exceptions: Three classes of 'discrepancies' (pp. 102-103): (1) monosyllabic roots such as /sa/ 'climb', which have no penult; (2) surface stress contrasts created by affixation, e.g. ['osa] 'one' vs [o-'sa] 'they climb', ['apa-na] 'saliva' vs [a-'pana] 'you feed', ['ai-a] 'you eat' vs [a'ia] 'king'; (3) an unexplained residue, some perhaps loans from Indonesian or neighbouring languages, with final or antepenultimate stress: ['aikune] 'beginning', [apa'lam] 'k.o. mango', [asu'wan] 'cassowary', [kari'sa] 'party', [kasi'pi] 'cassava', [sapa'u] 'ring', [sa'wan] 'sunny and drizzling', ['ukura] 'wrapped sago'; further definite loans are said to exist but are not listed. Because these are infrequent, stress is not written in the Nuaulu orthography.
new_statements.identity_note: Bolton's data are South Nuaulu [nxl] per the SIL archive record for the 1990 thesis (Glottolog lists iso_code 'nni; nxl' for the same reference); WALS code 'nua' maps to Glottolog sout2895 and gives both 'Nuaulu, North' and 'Nuaulu, South' as alternative names. Neither the 1989 paper's stress section nor the WALS page names a village or dialect beyond 'Nuaulu'.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation, the the domain quotation and the exception quote are all verbatim on printed pp.102-103 (PDF pp.111-112) of the held WILC vol.7 scan, exactly as the locator says; I read the rendered page image, not just the scanned. (2) The classification rests on a primary, fieldwork-based phonology article (Bolton 1989, SIL/Pattimura WILC 7) with an explicit stress section whose wording directly supports 'morphological' (root-penult, stress does not shift under prefixation or suffixation, surface antepenult with monosyllabic suffixes, contrastive pairs from affixation, secondary stress root-initial in 4+ syllable roots, listed lexical exceptions). Glottolog's descriptive bibliography has only two items, both by Bolton; the unheld one is her 1990 M.A. thesis, not available online per the SIL archive record downloaded now.
